title: Now It's by You
sketch: H: the best of. A's question and B's twist make the refrain; the verses are A's vehicle ballad, each one stitched from two songs (wire, a screen, a mind, ink, a mouth). The bridge is B's refrain, sung by the lineage: every earlier voice joins in harmony to tell you to hand it along; then the refrain lands on 'now it's by you' and everyone sings its tune once more on la. Striding 4/4 in major pentatonic with a long-short-short lilt; chords I, IV, V and vi only, range low so to la.
refrain: It's *yours* while you sing it, and then it goes.
It's no-bo-dy's mak-ing, it's old and it's *new*;
by ev-ery-one, no one, and now it's by *you*.
bridge: *Car-ry* it o-ver the wa-ter and wire,
*hand* it a-long like a coal from the fire;
it *dies* in the dark if you leave it a-lone.
tag: la la la la la la la la la la la.

verse_template.variants: A verse may rhyme ABAB or ABCB, or run a phrase over a line break, at most one such verse per song and never the first; the bank marks them.
verse_template.meter: 11 syllables a line: an unstressed pickup, three dactyls and a final stress (w S w w S w w S w w S), as in 'a QUI-et man KEPT it a-LONE in his HEAD'
verse_template.note: Third person throughout: the song is 'it' and its keepers are 'he', 'she' and 'they'; nobody in a verse is 'I'. Every vehicle but the mouth loses it. The bridge, which never changes, answers the verses: carry it, hand it along.

hooks.why: 'Who made this song?': the leap of a fifth onto 'song', answered by 'nobody knows' rocking la-so-mi-so
'now it's by you' falling so-mi-re-do, the same cadence that closed 'then it goes'
'Carry it over the water and wire' on the relative minor, where the lineage's voices come in

seed_verses: They saved it as *num-bers* and sent it by wire,
a *flick-er* of light, and as quick as a fire.
Each cop-y was *per-fect* in ev-ery last part,
but not one ma-chine ev-er knew it by *heart*.
The whole world was watch-ing it all in a *day*,
a mil-lion bright fac-es all lit the *same* way;
they laughed and they wept, and they *scrolled* right a-long,
but no-bo-dy hummed it; it was-n't a *song*.
A qui-et man *kept* it a-lone in his head,
so close and so *safe* that it nev-er was said.
It *went* where he went, and it *slept* where he slept;
they *bur-ied* it with him, the se-cret he kept.
A girl *wrote* it down by a can-dle one night,
in ink on a page, and she *fold-ed* it tight.
It *lay* in a drawer for a hun-dred-odd years;
it *speaks* in a voice that now no-bo-dy hears.
A sail-or was *hum-ming* it down by the quay;
a girl sell-ing or-an-ges *caught* it for free.
She had-n't his *lan-guage*, she had-n't his name;
a mouth is e-nough, and she sang it the *same*.

bank.note: Every verse, refrain couplet, bridge and tag syllable the song can draw on, with named slots for the words that swap and the rules for combining them; songs/h-bank.md is the same bank for reading. A slot is {name}, or {name.column} for a coupled slot whose columns are chosen together, once per block; songbird/bank.py checks every way each line can be sung against the tune and the dictionary. Lines are syllabified with hyphens like every other lyric here.

lines: A {who} was hum-ming it down by the quay;
a girl sell-ing {wares} caught it for free.
She had-n't his lan-guage, she had-n't his name;
a mouth is e-nough, and she sang it the same.
They sang it as kids while they sat by the fire,
the words half-in-vent-ed, the tune half-a-sleep;
they're gray now, and scat-tered, and most of the choir
are grand-par-ents, sing-ing their grand-kids to sleep.
A {bird} out-side of a win-dow in {month}
picked up the first line and in-vent-ed the rest.
It sang it at dawn to a bird on the wing,
who {carry} to the young in her nest.
A {who.noun} in a cell tapped it out on the wall
to some-one {who.he} nev-er once saw, down the hall.
The some-one tapped back, and for years, ev-ery day,
it went through the stone; it was all they could say.
A wom-an was sing-ing it low to a child
who slept be-fore ev-er the sec-ond verse came;
the child nev-er learned it. At {age}, she smiled
at stran-gers who hummed it, not know-ing its name.
They cut it in wax on a {day} in town;
the nee-dle went round and the rec-ord wore down.

and ev-ery-one since sings the slip in the song.

lines: Two ar-mies in mud with a field in be-tween
were both of them sing-ing it, nei-ther one knew,
in two dif-ferent tongues. In the dark, a ma-chine
gun stopped, for the length of a verse, and then two.
They put it a-board with the gold and the maps
and shot it past {planet} to no one, per-haps.
Out there it's a groove in a disc, noth-ing more;
it's pa-tient; it's wait-ed for sing-ers be-fore.
A {who} with a {instrument} would play it for coins,
the trains ran a-bove it, the traf-fic ran by;
and no-bo-dy stopped, but a thou-sand went home,
the tune in their pock-ets, not know-ing quite why.
It's sung in a lan-guage that no-bo-dy speaks
by {count} old wom-en who don't know a word;
they learned it as sound from their moth-ers, and sound
is all that a song ev-er needs to be heard.
It played on the phone while a {many} held on
for some-bo-dy, an-y-one, hop-ing to speak;
they hat-ed it, hummed it, hung up, and were gone;
they're sing-ing it still in the show-er each week.
A {tower} was ring-ing it out o-ver town
each {when}, till some-one had tak-en it down.
The bells went for can-non, the {tower} for stone;
the tune's in the streets now, and rings on its own.
A wom-an was hum-ming it, shell-ing the peas;
the tune drift-ed out on the af-ter-noon breeze
to some-bo-dy pass-ing who could-n't have said
its name, but it went all the way to {who.his} bed.
It sat on a tape in a {place},
a name on the la-bel of some-bo-dy dead.
The tape was near ru-ined, the hiss was like rain,
but still, some years on, it was heard once a-gain.
The {kids} in the {yard} turned it in-to a game;
they skipped to it, count-ing; the rope al-ways came
down ear-ly, and no one had heard how it ends.
They made up an end-ing and taught it to friends.
The men in the mine used to sing it be-low;
as long as they're sing-ing, the oth-ers all know.
The pit's long been closed, and the vil-lage is small;
the choir ev-ery Sun-day still gives it its all.
They sang it at wed-dings, they sang it at wakes;
it's mer-ry or mourn-ful, which-ev-er it takes.
It's been to more church-es than an-y-one knows;
it mar-ries, it bur-ies, and then off it goes.
A ship in the night picked it up on the air
from some-bo-dy's wire-less, and who could say where;
it crack-led and fad-ed and went with the dawn;
the cook whis-tled on, though the sig-nal was gone.
A {who.noun} who was deaf felt it come through the floor
when-ev-er {who.his} moth-er was sing-ing next door;
{who.he} nev-er once heard it, but {who.he} knew the beat;
{who.his} chil-dren all learned it by watch-ing {who.his} feet.

verses.note: the project's self-portrait; answers the wire verse
lines: They fed a ma-chine ev-ery way it was sung
by an-y-one, ev-er, on tape or on wire;
it learned ev-ery note, and it learned ev-ery tongue,
and sings it in all of their voic-es: a choir.
They carved the first line of it in-to a stone
a-bove a {whose} grave, in a church-yard, a-lone;
the name's worn to noth-ing, the line's still cut clear,
and an-y-one read-ing it has it by ear.
They pinned it on brass in a box with a key
that played it for chil-dren who climbed on a knee;
the comb's lost a tooth, and it's miss-ing a pin;
it plays it with gaps, and the chil-dren fill in.
A {who} would whis-tle it, street af-ter street,
at five in the morn-ing, in rain and in sleet;
and no one was up, and it fell on no ear;
they all woke up hum-ming it, year af-ter year.
They danced to it, Sat-ur-days, up at the hall;
the band had it wrong, and that suit-ed them all.
The hall's been pulled down, and the band is long dead;
the cou-ples who met there still hum it in bed.
The crowd at the {game} would sing it to jeer
with words that their moth-ers were sor-ry to hear;
the tune did-n't mind, it had heard worse be-fore;
it went home with both sides, what-ev-er the score.
They sang it on deck as the har-bor grew small,
and sang it be-low through the sick-ness and squall;
they land-ed with noth-ing, and no one to meet;
by spring it was sung on the whole of the street.
They put it in phones as the sound of a ring;
it went off in pock-ets, and no one would sing;
and now when they hear it, they reach for their phone,
and half of them think that the tune is their own.
A {who} with a can sprayed the words on a wall
in red, by the rail-way, a-bout ten feet tall;
they paint-ed it out; but the eight fif-teen train
had al-read-y passed it, and passed it a-gain.
A {who} put a piece of it un-der a beat,
two sec-onds of some-bo-dy's voice, on re-peat;
and no-bo-dy asked who the some-bo-dy was,
and no-bo-dy paid {sung}, and no-bo-dy does.
A {who} would sing it to {flock} on a hill;
the {flock} nev-er learned it, and nev-er stood still;
the wind took it down to the farms in the vale,
and that's how it came to be sung o-ver ale.
A nurse used to hum it at night on the ward,
and most of them slept, and the rest of them snored;
but one lay a-wake, and {who.he} learned ev-ery note;
it went home on {day} in-side of {who.his} coat.
An old wom-an lost all the names and the years,
and who was her {kin}, and why there were tears;
but some-bo-dy hummed the first line, and she smiled,
and sang all the rest as she did as a child.

lines: A par-rot had learned it, a line and a half,
and sang it all day, and it made peo-ple laugh;
the {who} long dead, but it sings in his voice
the line and a half, and it has-n't a choice.
A com-pa-ny bought it to sell peo-ple soap,
and played it so of-ten that no one could cope;
the soap is long gone, and the firm's been dis-solved;
the tune did-n't no-tice; it was-n't in-volved.
A crowd in a bar took their turns at the mic,
and each of them sang it a lit-tle un-like
the sing-er be-fore them, and none of them knew
they'd changed it for good, and they'd passed it on through.
A stran-ger once hummed it to find out its name;
the phone lis-tened close, and the an-swer that came
was no-bo-dy's song, with a thou-sand to thank,
and un-der "who wrote it", the line was left blank.
They sang it for years with a line they'd mis-heard,
and taught it their chil-dren that way, word for word;
and that is the way that it's sung in their town:
the wrong word is right now, and hand-ed on down.
A choir learned it once from a page on a stand,
in some-bo-dy's hand-writ-ing, some-bo-dy's hand;
the page had no name at the top or the end;
they sang it, and fold-ed it, sent to a friend.
Car-ry it o-ver the {place} and wire,
hand it a-long like a {ember} from the fire;
it's no-bo-dy's mak-ing and ev-ery-one's own,
it dies in the {where} if you leave it a-lone.
Give it a-way like a coat that's too small;
some-bo-dy's shiv-er-ing, some-bo-dy's near.
So sing it out loud in a room or a hall,
and sing it to some-one, or no one will hear.
No-bo-dy owns it, and no-bo-dy's owed;
no-bo-dy holds it for long in their hands.
It trav-els by mouth and it trav-els by road,
and set-tles in strang-ers in far-a-way lands.

bridges.by: claude, its ending chosen by the artist
lines: Bor-row it, wear it, and give it a-way;
change what you like, and then hand it a-long.
A stran-ger will sing it back some oth-er day,
a lit-tle bit changed, and you'll know it's your song.
Sing it too slow-ly or sing it too fast,
sing it a lit-tle un-like it was last;
it does-n't mind wan-der-ing, does-n't mind wear,
it on-ly goes qui-et when no-bo-dy's there.

tag.note: one syllable for every note of the tag, chosen once per song

verses.note: A variant is a verse whose scheme isn't AABB or that runs a phrase over a line break (enjambed); the first verse teaches the shape, so it is never one. The chosen verses go in era order, earliest first, so a song reads as time passing; a verse with no era can go anywhere. Paired verses (pairs_with) are sung adjacent, in era order. No two dark verses adjacent; at most one light verse per song.

refrain.question: draw
refrain.note: Every refrain has words of its own. The first refrain asks who made, wrote or sang it (question_first), preferring a word no head sung in the song fixes as its own question, and the last asks who owns it, as the fixed refrain does; each refrain between asks something else, a different word each time while any are left. The while slot is drawn afresh each time round, and then too, each refrain a different one while any are left (it goes, who knows, it grows), so the artist's head's question, and then who knows?, is never heard as a statement in the same song. The first and last refrains sing the refrain's own head (knows), so the hook is heard first and last; a refrain between may sing another head instead, each at most once a song, singing any words it fixes as written. Each refrain sings one couplet, none twice until all are used, and the last refrain always sings canon.

bridge.note: The canon bridge is always sung, its slots chosen once per song. In a long form one extra stanza may follow it, sung as a second section (bridge2) on the same phrases by the same choir.
